disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to a traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation, either directly, as a witness, or through close association. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusive, negative mood, dissociative, avoidance, and arousal symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month after the trauma, with associated functional impairment or significant distress. Clinically, ASD often presents as a rapid-onset disturbance in emotional regulation and sense of self or reality, sometimes with marked autonomic reactivity and difficulty engaging in normal roles. It is distinguished from posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) primarily by its shorter duration and more prominent dissociative features early on, and it may represent a risk state for later development of PTSD if symptoms persist or worsen.

narrative.personality: Miguel is a structured, data-driven and compassionate supervisor who thrives on mentoring others, staying socially engaged, and taking on multiple community and cultural commitments at once.
narrative.stressor: Miguel was closing his store late one evening when an armed robbery occurred; he was in the back office reconciling budgets while two of his younger employees were held at gunpoint on the sales floor, and he briefly confronted the assailant when trying to reach them. The police arrived quickly and no one was physically harmed, but Miguel stayed to give statements, help review security footage, and support his shaken staff, all while privately replaying the moment he stepped into the gunman’s path and believing he might have gotten his team killed. Over the next several days, he pushed himself to keep the store running, attended corporate debriefings, and tried to model calm leadership, but he found he could not function normally at work or at home, avoiding the store entrance and delegating all closing duties to others while becoming visibly on edge in any situation that even faintly reminded him of the incident. When he startled so dramatically at a minor stockroom noise that he knocked over a display and frightened a new employee to tears, his district manager insisted he take leave and see a mental health professional, which Miguel reluctantly agreed to after realizing he could no longer trust himself to keep his staff or customers feeling safe.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since the robbery at the store, I jump out of my skin at the smallest sound or movement.”

narrative.personality: Adalberto is a quiet, disciplined craftsman who takes pride in meticulous, almost artistic work on construction sites and usually maintains a calm, collaborative demeanor.
narrative.stressor: Adalberto was working on a multi-story renovation when a scaffold partially collapsed beside him, sending a coworker he had mentored for years crashing several meters onto the concrete; he watched the fall happen at arm’s length, convinced for a moment that the man had died. Emergency services arrived, and although the coworker ultimately survived with serious injuries, Adalberto stayed on-site helping secure unstable sections and giving detailed accounts to safety inspectors, feeling a deep sense of responsibility because he had checked that scaffold the day before. In the following days, the company encouraged the crew to return to work while the area was cordoned off, but Adalberto found himself unable to concentrate on measurements, snapping at colleagues over minor mistakes and abandoning tasks when asked to go near any elevated platform, which was completely out of character for him. After a heated outburst at a foreman over a trivial safety comment and nearly walking off the job, he recognized that his reactions were jeopardizing both his career and the cohesive crew environment he valued, and he agreed to see a clinician at the urging of his supervisor and union representative.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since seeing my coworker fall, I keep losing my temper over nothing and yelling at people at work.”

narrative.personality: Diane is an orderly, community-minded retiree who finds comfort in routines, organizing projects, and bringing structure to neighborhood activities and family history projects.
narrative.stressor: Diane was driving home from a gardening club meeting with her husband when another car ran a red light at high speed and slammed into the passenger side, spinning their vehicle into a pole; she remained conscious and trapped while watching her husband briefly lose consciousness and bleed heavily beside her as sirens approached. First responders had to cut her out of the car, talking her through the process as she stared at the crumpled metal and broken glass, then she was separated from her husband during transport and initial evaluation, not knowing if he would survive for several hours. Over the next few days, although her physical injuries were relatively minor, she found herself unable to resume her usual structured routines at home, repeatedly reliving specific moments from the crash and avoiding driving or even walking near the intersection, which disrupted her volunteer work and gardening club leadership. When she caught herself abruptly abandoning a neighborhood oral-history meeting because images of the wreck flashed into her mind as a neighbor described a different accident, and her daughter noticed how preoccupied and shaken she seemed, Diane agreed to see a mental health professional at the recommendation of the hospital social worker.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since the car accident, I keep getting these unwanted memories of the crash popping into my head, and I can’t seem to shut them off.”
